summary: This document describes Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR), a mechanism to minimize packet loss when a fault hits the IP network carrying multicast services such as IPTV. It is informational and describes a technique rather than a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7431 describes a way of protecting live multicast streams such as television. The router that delivers the stream to the viewers joins it over two different paths and keeps both open. It only forwards the copy from the first path, so nothing is duplicated and no extra bandwidth is used. When the first path breaks, the router starts forwarding the copy it was already receiving on the second path.

subtitle: Keeping multicast traffic flowing through a failure by sending it down two paths at once.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails, multicast traffic stops until the routing protocols notice and rebuild the tree, and that can take long enough to be visible to the viewer.
tldr.mechanism: Multicast-only Fast Reroute makes the router that joins a multicast stream join it twice, over two separate paths. It forwards only the copy from the primary path, so no traffic is duplicated, and when the primary fails it simply starts using the copy it was already receiving.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is informational and describes a technique rather than a standard. It needs no changes to the multicast protocols themselves, so it can be enabled on one router at a time.

facts.label: Suitable topologies
facts.value: Dual-plane networks, data centers with meshed layers

today: RFC 7431 is an Informational RFC published in August 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a technique rather than a protocol, and because it requires no changes to PIM or mLDP it can be enabled on one router at a time.

sections.title: Two Paths, One Stream
sections.content:
Different solutions have been developed and deployed to improve service guarantees, both for multicast video traffic and video on demand. Most of them are geared towards finding an alternate path around one or more failed network elements, whether link, node or path failures.

This document describes a mechanism for minimising packet loss when node or link failures occur. Multicast-only Fast Reroute works by making simple changes to the way selected routers use multicast protocols such as PIM and mLDP. No changes to the protocols themselves are required, and in many cases the multicast routing protocols do not have to depend on, or wait on, the unicast routing protocols to detect network failures.

On a merge point, the MoFRR logic determines a primary upstream multicast hop and a secondary one, and joins the tree via both simultaneously. Data packets are received over the primary and the secondary path, but only the packets from the primary hop are accepted and forwarded down the tree; the packets from the secondary hop are discarded. The way the hops are determined differs for PIM and for mLDP. When a failure is detected on the path to the primary hop, the repair happens by changing the secondary hop into the primary and the primary into the secondary. Because the repair is local, it is fast, which greatly improves convergence times when a node or link fails on the path to the primary hop.
sections.plainLanguage: The trick is that the second copy is already there before anything breaks. So when the first path dies, the router does not have to find a new one; it just starts using the copy it has been throwing away.

sections.title: Choosing the Backup Path
sections.content:
The basic idea is for a merge point router to join a multicast tree via two divergent upstream paths, to get as much redundancy as possible. To maximise robustness against any failure, the two paths should be as diverse as possible, and ideally they should not merge again upstream. Sometimes the topology guarantees this; other times extra configuration or techniques are needed.

A merge point should only accept and forward on one of the upstream paths at a time, to avoid forwarding the same packet twice. The choice of primary and secondary hop is made by the MoFRR logic and is normally based on unicast routing, which is how loop-free candidates are found. The secondary hop is a loop-free alternate, in the sense that RFC 5286 gives: an alternate next-hop that can be used to reach the destination without using the protected link or node.

In ECMP-mode, the interior gateway protocol installs two equal-cost paths to the source, and the loop-free alternate is then a primary next-hop. If the multicast tree is enabled for ECMP-mode MoFRR, the router installs those paths as the primary and the secondary hop. Before any failure, only packets received from the primary path are processed and packets from the secondary are dropped. The selected primary hop should be the same as it would be if the extension were not enabled, so that turning MoFRR on does not change normal routing. If more than two equal-cost paths exist, one is chosen as primary and another as secondary, and the choice is a local decision, although information from the link-state topology could be used to make the two paths as divergent as possible so that they do not lead to the same upstream node. MoFRR does not restrict how many paths are joined.

In non-ECMP-mode, a router joins a primary path to its primary hop and a secondary path to its loop-free alternate hop. To prevent control-plane loops, a router must stop joining the secondary hop if that hop is the only member in the outgoing interface list. The reason is a feedback loop between two neighbouring routers: if both have received a request for a multicast tree, they each join the primary path on their own plane and a secondary path to the neighbour, and if their receivers then leave at the same time, the two trees can keep each other alive, because a secondary path join is not distinguishable from a primary join.
sections.plainLanguage: The backup path has to be a real alternative, and it has to be chosen so that turning the feature on does not change which path normal traffic uses.

sections.title: How Each Protocol Picks Its Hop
sections.content:
An upstream multicast hop is a candidate next-hop that can be used to reach the root of the tree. It is normally based on unicast routing, which is how loop-free candidates are found. With MoFRR the procedures select a primary and a backup hop, and the procedures differ between the two multicast protocols.

For PIM, the selection of the upstream hop is the reverse path forwarding procedure. Based on a unicast route lookup on either the source address or the rendezvous point, an upstream interface is selected both for sending the joins and prunes and for accepting the multicast packets. The interface on which the packets are received is what is used to pass or fail the reverse path forwarding check, and packets received on an interface that was not selected as the primary are discarded.

For mLDP the selection also depends on unicast routing, but the difference is that acceptance of multicast packets is based on MPLS labels rather than on the interface on which the packet arrived. Following the procedures in the mLDP specification, an upstream label switching router is elected, and that elected router is given a unique local MPLS label for the path. Multicast packets are forwarded only if their MPLS label matches the label allocated for that path's primary upstream router.
sections.plainLanguage: Both protocols work out which way is upstream by looking at unicast routes, but they differ in how a packet proves it arrived from the right place: PIM checks the port it came in on, mLDP checks a label on the packet.

sections.title: Noticing That the Primary Path Has Failed
sections.content:
Once the two paths are established, the next step is detecting a failure on the primary path, so that the router knows when to switch to the backup. The RFC describes four possibilities.

The first and simplest is to detect the failure of the local interface, as is done for unicast fast reroute. Detection can use the loss of signal or the loss of probing packets, for example with bidirectional forwarding detection. This option can be combined with the others, and just as for unicast fast reroute a 50 millisecond switchover is possible.

The second option compares the packets received on the primary and secondary streams but forwards only one of them, the first to arrive, whichever interface it came in on. This can give zero packet loss for streams based on the real-time transport protocol.

The third option assumes a minimum known packet rate for a given data stream. If a packet does not arrive on the primary within that time frame, the router assumes the primary path has failed and switches to the secondary. A 50 millisecond switchover may be possible for high-rate streams, for example internet television where standard definition video has a continuous inter-packet gap of about 3 milliseconds, but in general the delay depends on the rate of the multicast stream.

The fourth option leans on the improvements in interior gateway protocol convergence speed. When the primary path to the source is withdrawn by the interior gateway protocol, the router switches to the backup path and the upstream hop becomes the secondary one. Because the secondary path is already in place, and assuming it is disjoint from the primary path, the convergence time does not include the time needed to build a new tree, and is therefore smaller. A sub-second to sub-200 millisecond switchover should be possible.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to notice the break, from watching the physical link to waiting for the routing protocol to give up on the path. The quickest depends on how fast the failure shows up locally.

sections.title: Where This Works Best
sections.content:
MoFRR is topology dependent, and its applicability is the same as that of loop-free alternate fast reroute. It works best in dual-plane topologies, where a primary plane and a secondary plane are fully disjoint from each other all the way into the points of presence. This two-plane design is common in service provider networks, because it removes single points of failure in the core. Multicast streams, especially for densely watched channels, typically flow along both planes anyway, and the only change MoFRR adds is on the links where the provider edge routers join a secondary path to their secondary equal-cost hop. Each provider edge router then receives two copies of the same stream, and the copy from the secondary hop is discarded. When a router detects a routing failure on the path to its primary hop it switches to the secondary, and it may switch back if the failure is repaired. The primary and secondary hops have only local context, not end-to-end context.

The RFC gives four reasons why MoFRR is appealing in such topologies. It is easy to deploy and simple, because the functionality is only required on the provider edge devices, each of which can be enabled separately with no network-wide coordination, and interoperability testing is not needed because there are no protocol changes. It gives end-to-end failure detection and recovery, because any failure along the path from the source to the provider edge can be detected and repaired with the secondary disjoint stream. It is capacity efficient, because the secondary path grafts onto the normal multicast trees at the aggregation level and so demands no extra capacity on the distribution links or in the backbone; this differs from conventional fast reroute mechanisms, which often duplicate capacity when the backup path crosses links that already carry the primary tree. And it is loop-free, because the secondary path join is sent on an equal-cost disjoint path, so the neighbour receiving it is closer to the source and cannot cause a loop.

Two further topologies are described. A provider edge router can be dual-homed to a dual-plane backbone with two disjoint equal-cost paths to the source, which is the ECMP case. Or provider edge routers can be connected in pairs, each connected to a different plane, with only one shortest path to the source; here the secondary path is offered to the peer in the other plane, which is the non-ECMP case and needs the extended neighbour selection. Where the network is not dual-plane, the secondary path may be affected by the same failure as the primary, and there is then no guarantee of uninterrupted traffic without loss or duplication. Capacity planning tools can simulate whether each provider edge router can build two disjoint branches of the same tree, for hundreds of routers and hundreds of sources, and the designer can then add links or change metrics to improve the coverage.
sections.plainLanguage: This works best in networks built with two separate planes, so that a cut in one leaves the other untouched. It is cheap there, because the spare path uses capacity that is already there.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The RFC states that there are no security considerations for this design other than those already in the main PIM specification and the mLDP specification. That is consistent with the design itself, since MoFRR changes no protocol messages and adds no new signalling.

One operational consequence is worth noting, though it is not a security matter. Because a MoFRR router only accepts packets from the primary path and discards packets from the secondary path, management applications such as ping and mtrace will not work when verifying the secondary path. The principle may also be applied to multicast virtual private networks.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing new to secure, because nothing new is sent. The only practical oddity is that the tools you would use to test the spare path will not work, since the router throws those packets away.

messages.note: When the primary path fails, the backup becomes the primary. Only the merge point has to act.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO NOTICE THE FAILURE

cells: Loss of signal, or loss of BFD probes
Compare the packets on both paths and forward the first to arrive
Zero packet loss for RTP streams
No packet on the primary within the expected interval
50 msec for high-rate streams; IPTV has about a 3 msec inter-packet gap
The unicast routing protocol withdraws the primary path

viz.caption: WHY IT IS ATTRACTIVE IN A DUAL-PLANE NETWORK

items.title: Easy to deploy
items.text: Only the edge devices need it, each can be enabled on its own, and no protocol changes mean no interoperability testing.

items.title: End-to-end recovery
items.text: Any failure on the way from the source to the edge can be repaired with the second, disjoint stream.

items.title: Capacity efficient
items.text: The spare path grafts onto the trees that are already there, so no extra capacity is needed.

items.title: Loop-free
items.text: The backup join goes to a neighbour that is closer to the source, so it cannot create a loop.
